concepts.title: The JVM & Bytecode: How Java Actually Runs
concepts.description: Java source code is compiled to platform-independent bytecode, not native machine code, and the JVM interprets (and later JIT-compiles) that bytecode at run time -- a two-step model that explains 'write once, run anywhere', why some errors only show up when you run a program rather than when you compile it, and what a JVM, JRE, and JDK each actually are.
learningObjectives: Describe the full pipeline from a .java source file to a running program: compilation to bytecode, class loading, and JVM execution.
Explain why Java bytecode is platform-independent while code compiled directly to native machine instructions (as in C) is not.
Explain the relationship between the JVM, the JRE, and the JDK.
Explain what Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation is and why the JVM bothers with it instead of only interpreting.
Predict what javac and java each do, and explain why a source file's name is tied to its public class name.
Distinguish a compile-time error from a run-time error in terms of which tool catches it and when.

sections.heading: From .java to .class: What javac Actually Produces
Bytecode: An Intermediate Language, Not Machine Code
sections.body:
Bytecode is deliberately not tied to any real CPU. It's an instruction set for an imaginary stack-based machine -- opcodes like `iload`, `iadd`, `invokevirtual`, `areturn` -- that every conforming JVM implementation agrees to understand, regardless of whether that JVM is running on an x86 Windows laptop, an ARM Mac, or a Linux server. This is the entire mechanism behind Java's famous "write once, run anywhere" promise: the *same* `.class` file, byte-for-byte, can run unmodified on any machine that has a compatible JVM installed, because the JVM -- not your compiled output -- is the piece that knows how to talk to that particular machine's actual hardware.

Contrast this with a language like C, where the compiler produces native machine code directly -- actual x86 or ARM instructions -- during compilation. That's fast to run with no extra runtime translation step, but the resulting binary is tied to the CPU architecture and often the OS it was built for; a Linux ELF binary compiled for x86-64 will not run on a Windows machine or an ARM Mac at all. Java pushes that machine-specific translation later, to run time, in exchange for portability of the compiled artifact. It's worth being precise about what portability actually means here: it's the bytecode that's portable, not some claim that Java needs zero runtime infrastructure -- you still need a JVM installed on the target machine, matching or newer than the version the bytecode was compiled for.

sections.heading: The JVM at Run Time: Classloading, Interpretation, and JIT Compilation
sections.body:
Running `java Hello` kicks off a distinct pipeline from compilation. First, the JVM's **classloader** locates `Hello.class` and reads its bytecode into memory. Before running anything, a **bytecode verifier** checks that the bytecode is well-formed and doesn't violate the JVM's safety rules (you can't, for instance, ship bytecode that reads memory it was never given access to) -- this is part of why a JVM can run bytecode from an untrusted source with more confidence than blindly executing an arbitrary native binary would allow.

Execution itself starts out by **interpreting** the bytecode: the JVM reads each instruction and carries out its effect, one at a time, much like a human following a recipe line by line. That's simple and starts instantly, but it re-does the work of interpreting the same instructions every time a loop or a frequently-called method runs. So modern JVMs (HotSpot, the default in OpenJDK, is the canonical example) also run a **Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler** in the background, which profiles the running program, notices which methods are actually 'hot' (called often), and compiles *those specific methods* down to real native machine code for the CPU it's actually running on -- swapping the interpreted version out for the compiled one transparently, mid-execution. This is why long-running Java server processes often measurably speed up a few seconds or minutes after starting: the JIT hasn't 'warmed up' and optimized the hot paths yet at the very start. It's a deliberate middle ground between pure interpretation (portable, slow) and pure ahead-of-time native compilation (fast, not portable) -- Java gets a portable artifact and still gets native-speed execution for the parts of the program that matter most, just a little later than start-up.

sections.heading: JVM vs JRE vs JDK: Clearing Up the Alphabet Soup
sections.body:
These three terms describe layers, not synonyms. The **JVM** (Java Virtual Machine) is the actual execution engine -- the thing that loads, verifies, interprets, and JIT-compiles bytecode; it's a specification with multiple implementations (HotSpot being the most common). The **JRE** (Java Runtime Environment) is the JVM *plus* the core standard library classes a compiled program needs to actually run (things like `String`, `ArrayList`, I/O classes) -- enough to run a compiled Java program, but no compiler. The **JDK** (Java Development Kit) is the JRE *plus* the tools you need to actually develop Java software: `javac` (the compiler), `jar` (packaging), `javadoc`, a debugger, and so on.

In practice, standalone JRE-only distributions have become rare -- essentially every developer just installs a JDK, which includes everything needed both to write and to run Java code, and production deployments increasingly ship custom minimal runtimes built from a JDK using tools like `jlink` rather than distributing a separate generic JRE. The three-letter distinction still matters conceptually, though, because it maps directly onto the pipeline: you need a JDK to turn `.java` into `.class` (that's `javac`, a JDK tool), and you need at least a JVM present to actually execute that `.class` file (that's the JRE's job, at minimum).

sections.heading: Compile-Time vs Run-Time: Two Separate Moments Where Things Can Fail
sections.body:
Because compilation and execution are genuinely separate steps carried out by separate tools (`javac` vs `java`), Java bugs split cleanly into two categories depending on *when* they're caught. Syntax errors, type mismatches, and undeclared variables are caught by `javac` at **compile time** -- the program never even produces a `.class` file, so it can never be run in a broken state for these specific classes of mistakes. But plenty of problems are invisible to the compiler because they depend on values or conditions that only exist while the program is actually running: dividing by a variable that happens to be zero, calling a method on a reference that happens to be `null`, or accessing an array index that happens to be out of bounds. These surface only at **run time**, as exceptions thrown by the JVM while it's executing your bytecode -- `javac` compiled the code just fine because there was nothing syntactically or type-wise wrong with it.

This is a genuinely useful lens for reading Java error messages: if the error appears when you run `javac`, the problem is structural and the program never ran at all; if it appears when you run `java` (a stack trace, an exception name, a nonzero exit code), the program *did* start executing and failed partway through, which usually means the bug depends on specific data or a specific code path, not a universal defect in every possible execution.

examples.title: The Two-Step Pipeline: javac Then java
examples.explanation: `javac Hello.java` and `java Hello` are two entirely different programs doing two entirely different jobs, and mixing them up is a very common early confusion. `javac` is a compiler: it reads source text, checks it, and writes a `.class` file -- it does not run your program, and a silent, output-free success is completely normal and expected. `java` is the launcher for the JVM: it takes a class *name* (not a file name -- note there's no `.class` or `.java` suffix in `java Hello`), locates the corresponding `.class` file via the classloader, and executes its bytecode starting from `main`. If you run `java Hello` before `javac Hello.java` has ever succeeded, there is no bytecode to find yet, and you'll get an error about a missing or unloadable class -- a very different failure from a compiler error, because it's the *runtime* telling you it has nothing to execute.

examples.title: A Compile-Time Error vs a Run-Time Error, Side by Side
examples.explanation: The commented-out line would fail at `javac` time with a type-mismatch error, because dividing an `int` by a `String` is nonsensical in a way the compiler can detect just by looking at the declared types -- the program would never even produce a `.class` file. The active line, `total / divisor`, is completely legal from the compiler's point of view: dividing one `int` by another `int` is a perfectly valid operation in general. The problem here is a *value*, not a *type* -- `divisor` happens to be `0` -- and the compiler has no way to know that ahead of time by just reading the code. So this program compiles cleanly, and only fails once the JVM actually executes that division at run time, throwing `ArithmeticException: / by zero`. Same file, two very different kinds of bugs, caught by two different tools at two different moments.

examples.title: Peeking at Real Bytecode with javap
examples.explanation: `javap -c` disassembles a compiled `.class` file back into readable bytecode instructions, and it's a genuinely useful way to make the source-to-bytecode idea concrete rather than abstract. `iload_0` and `iload_1` push the method's first and second `int` parameters onto an internal operand stack; `iadd` pops the top two stack values, adds them, and pushes the result back; `ireturn` pops that result and returns it to the caller as an `int`. Notice there's no concept of `a` or `b` as named variables anymore, no `+` operator, no `return` keyword -- just numbered local slots and a tiny fixed vocabulary of stack operations. This is the actual, portable artifact that ships inside `Adder.class` and that every JVM, on every operating system, agrees on how to execute; your readable Java source is purely a convenience for humans that `javac` throws away once it's done its job.

misconceptions.description: Java is a purely interpreted language, similar to a scripting language, with no compilation step involved at all.
misconceptions.clarification: Java involves two distinct translation steps, not zero and not one. `javac` performs a real, ahead-of-time compilation from source text to bytecode before the program ever runs -- this is not skipped or optional, and it's where most syntax and type errors are caught. Then, at run time, the JVM itself further translates that bytecode, initially by interpreting it and increasingly by JIT-compiling hot methods into native machine code. So Java is neither 'purely interpreted' (there's a genuine ahead-of-time compile step producing a persistent artifact, the .class file) nor 'purely compiled to native code ahead of time' (that final native-code step, when it happens at all, happens later, at run time, and only for code the JVM decides is worth it).

misconceptions.description: Since Java's bytecode is platform-independent, a compiled .class file will run on any computer, even one with no Java installed at all.
misconceptions.clarification: "Write once, run anywhere" describes the portability of the *bytecode artifact* across machines that already have a compatible JVM -- it does not mean the JVM itself is unnecessary. A `.class` file is not executable on its own; some JVM has to be present on the target machine to load, verify, and run it. There's a second, sharper version of this same misconception worth flagging: bytecode compiled by a newer JDK is stamped with a class file version, and an older JVM will refuse to run bytecode compiled for a newer Java version than it supports -- so portability across operating systems is real, but it's not unconditional portability across every JVM version too.

exercises.prompt: A student saves the code below in a file named MainApp.java and runs `javac MainApp.java`. Compilation fails with: `error: class Hello is public, should be declared in a file named Hello.java`. Explain the bug and fix it.
hints: Nothing is syntactically wrong with the code inside the class -- read the error message again: what does it say the file should be named?
Java has a strict rule tying a top-level public class to the exact name of the file that contains it. Which identifier in this code has to match the file name?
You can fix this two ways: rename the file to match the class, or rename the class to match the file. Which one is the idiomatic choice here?
exercises.solutionExplanation: The class itself compiles fine in isolation -- the bug is entirely about the mismatch between the file name (MainApp.java) and the name of the public class it contains (Hello). javac enforces a strict naming contract for top-level public classes specifically because the JVM's classloader later needs a predictable way to find a class by name; allowing arbitrary file names for public classes would break that lookup. The idiomatic fix is to rename the file to Hello.java rather than renaming the class to MainApp, since the class name is usually the more meaningful, intentional choice and the file name is just where it happens to live.

exercises.prompt: Alice successfully compiles this program with `javac Calculator.java`, which produces Calculator.class. She then deletes Calculator.java (keeping only the compiled Calculator.class) and runs `java Calculator`. What happens, and why?
hints: Once javac has already produced Calculator.class successfully, does the java launcher need the original .java text at all to run the program?
Think about exactly what java loads and executes: is it your source code, or the bytecode sitting in the .class file?
The .java source file is only ever read by javac, at compile time -- java's job starts and ends with bytecode that already exists.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It runs perfectly fine and prints 'Result: 5'. The .java source file is not needed to run the program once compilation has already succeeded and produced Calculator.class -- java only needs the bytecode.
exercises.solutionExplanation: javac's entire job is to translate source text into a .class file; once that file exists, it's a self-contained artifact that no longer depends on the source that produced it. `java Calculator` tells the JVM to find a class named Calculator (via the classloader, which looks for Calculator.class in the classpath) and execute its bytecode starting at main -- it never reads or needs Calculator.java at all. So deleting the source file after a successful compile has zero effect on running the already-compiled program; it would only matter if you later needed to recompile (say, to fix a bug or change behavior), since at that point the source is gone and there's nothing for javac to compile.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following best explains why a compiled Java .class file can run unmodified on Windows, macOS, and Linux, while a compiled C program generally cannot?
options: Java source code is inherently simpler than C source code, so it happens to run everywhere without any extra work.

javac compiles Java source into bytecode, a machine-independent instruction set that any conforming JVM interprets or JIT-compiles into that specific machine's native instructions at run time -- whereas a C compiler produces native machine code tied to a specific OS and CPU architecture already, at compile time.
Java programs are never compiled at all, so there is no machine-specific translation step to worry about.
The JVM re-reads and re-parses the original .java source text directly every time the program runs, skipping bytecode entirely.
assessments.explanation: Option B correctly identifies the actual mechanism: javac's output (bytecode) is deliberately machine-independent, and the machine-specific translation step is deferred to run time, performed by whichever JVM happens to be running on that particular machine -- that's exactly what makes the same .class file usable across operating systems. Option A is wrong because portability has nothing to do with source complexity. Option C is wrong because Java absolutely does have a compilation step (javac); it's just not the final, machine-specific one. Option D is wrong on two counts: the JVM works from bytecode, not source text, and it does not re-parse source on every run -- the whole point of compiling ahead of time is to avoid that.

assessments.prompt: A new engineer coming from a language like Python, where you just run a .py file directly, asks you to explain exactly what happens between typing `javac Hello.java` and seeing 'Hello, Java!' printed after running `java Hello`. Give a full explanation of the compilation and execution model, including the specific role the JVM plays.
assessments.modelAnswer: There are two genuinely separate steps here, run by two different tools. First, `javac Hello.java` is the compiler: it reads the Java source text, checks it for syntax errors and type mismatches, and -- if everything checks out -- writes a new file, Hello.class, containing bytecode: a compact set of instructions for an abstract, portable machine defined by the JVM specification, not real CPU instructions. This step produces no output and no running program by itself; it's purely a translation, and it's also where most 'silly' mistakes (typos, wrong types, mismatched braces) get caught, before the program has ever executed a single line. Second, `java Hello` launches the JVM and tells it to run the class named Hello. The JVM's classloader finds Hello.class, a bytecode verifier checks that it's well-formed and safe, and then the JVM begins executing it starting from the main method -- initially by interpreting the bytecode instruction by instruction, and, for code that turns out to run frequently, by JIT-compiling it into real native machine code on the fly for extra speed. This whole model exists because bytecode, unlike a C compiler's native output, is not tied to any specific operating system or CPU -- the exact same Hello.class file could be handed to a JVM running on Windows, macOS, or Linux and it would run correctly on each, because it's each machine's own JVM that does the final, machine-specific translation, not javac. The tradeoff for that portability is that you need a JVM installed on any machine that's going to run compiled Java, which is a genuinely different model from a language that has no separate compiled artifact at all.

assessments.prompt: A single file named Shapes.java contains: class Circle { } followed by public class Shapes { public static void main(String[] args) { } }. What happens when you run javac Shapes.java?
options: Compilation fails, because a .java file may contain at most one class definition, public or not.

Compilation succeeds and produces both Circle.class and Shapes.class, because the file name only has to match the one public top-level class it contains -- Circle is a perfectly legal package-private class living in the same file.
Compilation fails, because Circle must also be declared public once the file already contains a public class.
Compilation fails, because Circle is defined before Shapes, and Java requires the public class to be declared first in a file.
assessments.explanation: The file-naming rule only constrains the one public top-level class in a file: the file name must match that class's name exactly. It says nothing about whether other, non-public classes may share the same file -- they can, freely, as long as none of them is also public. Circle has no access modifier here, making it package-private, which coexists perfectly legally with the public class Shapes in Shapes.java. Option A is wrong because multiple classes per file is routine, not forbidden. Option C is wrong because there's no rule that every class in a file must share the public class's visibility. Option D is wrong because Java imposes no ordering requirement among classes in a file based on which one happens to be public.

assessments.prompt: A long-running Java server process handles requests noticeably faster after running for several minutes than it did in its first few seconds, even though the workload and code never changed. What actually explains this?
options: The JVM periodically re-reads and recompiles the original .java source files, looking for new optimization opportunities as it goes.

The JVM starts out interpreting bytecode instruction by instruction; its JIT compiler profiles execution in the background, identifies methods that are called often, and compiles just those hot methods into native machine code, transparently swapping them in for the interpreted version once ready.
The operating system's disk cache is the entire explanation -- once .class files are cached in memory, the JVM's own execution strategy has nothing further to do with the speedup.
Bytecode verification runs on every single method call until the JVM decides the program is safe, after which it stops, accounting for the entire speedup.
assessments.explanation: This is exactly the JIT warm-up effect described in the material: execution begins with plain interpretation, which is portable and starts instantly but redoes the same work on every pass through a loop or frequently-called method. The JIT compiler runs alongside it, profiling which methods are actually hot and compiling just those down to native machine code for the specific CPU the program is running on, then swapping the compiled version in without the program noticing. Option A is wrong because the JVM never re-reads or recompiles source text -- javac's job is already finished long before the JVM starts running anything. Option C is wrong because disk caching of .class files happens once, near start-up, and cannot account for a gradual speedup over minutes. Option D is wrong because bytecode verification is a one-time, per-class check done at class-loading time, not a per-call cost that tapers off.

assessments.prompt: Consider two separate problems in two separate programs: (1) int x = "five"; and (2) int[] nums = new int[3]; int y = nums[5]; Which statement correctly describes when each problem is caught?
options: Both are caught by javac at compile time, since array bounds and type mismatches are both fully determined just by reading the source.

Problem (1) is a compile-time type error -- javac rejects assigning a String to an int and never produces a .class file at all; problem (2) compiles successfully because the index is only known to exceed the array's bounds once the program actually runs, throwing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at run time.
Both are only caught at run time, because javac performs no type checking of any kind.
Problem (1) compiles fine because Java automatically converts string literals that look numeric; problem (2) is a compile-time error because the array's size, 3, is a fixed, known constant.
assessments.explanation: This tracks the compile-time vs run-time split directly: a type mismatch like assigning a String to an int variable is visible to javac just by looking at the declared types, with no need to run anything, so it's rejected before any .class file is produced. Whether index 5 is out of bounds for a length-3 array, though, depends on the actual runtime value of the index and the actual runtime size of the array -- information the compiler doesn't try to track for arbitrary array accesses -- so this compiles cleanly and only fails when the JVM actually executes that specific access. Option A overstates what javac checks. Option C is wrong because javac absolutely does perform type checking; that's a large part of what it does. Option D has both halves backwards -- there's no auto-conversion from String to int, and array-bounds checking is never done at compile time in Java.

concepts.title: Static Typing, Primitives, and Reference Types
concepts.description: Java's compiler commits every variable to a fixed type at compile time; primitive types store a raw value directly while reference types store the address of an object living elsewhere -- and that single distinction quietly shapes how assignment, equality, method calls, and default values all behave.
learningObjectives: Declare variables with explicit types and explain what it means for Java to be statically typed, contrasted with dynamically-typed languages.
List Java's primitive types and explain what 'primitive' means in terms of what a variable's storage actually holds.
Explain the difference between a primitive variable and a reference variable in terms of what is stored in the variable itself.
Predict the difference between == on primitives versus == on reference types, including the String literal pool trap.
Use arithmetic, relational, logical, and compound assignment operators correctly, including integer division and short-circuit evaluation.
Explain what happens when one reference variable is assigned to another (aliasing) as opposed to assigning one primitive to another (copying).

sections.heading: Static Typing: The Compiler Commits to a Type Up Front
sections.body:
In Java, every variable is declared with a specific type, and that type is fixed for the entire lifetime of that variable: `int count = 5;` means `count` can only ever hold `int` values, forever, and the compiler checks every single assignment and expression involving `count` against that fact before the program ever runs. Try to assign a `String` to it later and `javac` rejects the program outright -- there's no path to running it in that broken state.

This is a genuinely different model from dynamically-typed languages like Python or JavaScript, where a variable is just a name that can be rebound to a value of any type at any point, and a type mismatch (like trying to add a number to a string in a way the language doesn't support) only surfaces as an error once that specific line actually executes, potentially deep into production use if that code path is rarely hit. Java's static typing trades some flexibility for catching an entire category of bugs earlier and more reliably -- the cost is showing up on the type, everywhere, even when it feels obvious. Java 10 introduced `var` for local variables (`var count = 5;`), which lets the compiler *infer* the type from the right-hand side instead of you writing it explicitly -- but this is purely a convenience for the programmer typing less; the type is still fixed and checked exactly as strictly as if you'd written `int` yourself. `var` does not make Java dynamically typed for that variable.

sections.heading: Primitive Types: The Value Lives Directly in the Variable
Reference Types: The Variable Holds an Address, Not the Object
sections.body:
Anything that isn't one of those eight primitives -- every class type, every array, `String` included -- is a **reference type**. A reference variable's storage location does not hold the object itself; it holds a reference (conceptually, an address) pointing to where the actual object lives, separately, on the heap. This has a direct, observable consequence: assigning one reference variable to another doesn't copy the object -- it copies the address, so both variables end up pointing at the exact same object.

```java
int[] original = {1, 2, 3};
int[] alias = original;   // copies the REFERENCE, not the array's contents
alias[0] = 99;
System.out.println(original[0]);   // 99 -- both names point at the same array
```

Compare that to two primitive variables, where assignment genuinely copies the value, and the two variables become completely independent afterward. This primitive-vs-reference split is arguably the single most consequential distinction in the whole language -- it resurfaces in method calls (does mutating a parameter affect the caller's variable?), in equality checks (next section), and eventually in understanding how objects and collections behave. `null` is the literal that means 'this reference variable currently points at nothing at all' -- only reference variables can be `null`; a primitive like `int` can never be `null`, it always holds an actual value.

sections.heading: Operators: Arithmetic, the Integer Division Trap, and Short-Circuiting
sections.body:
The arithmetic operators (`+ - * / %`) behave mostly as expected, with one sharp edge: dividing two integer types performs **integer division**, truncating any fractional part rather than rounding -- `7 / 2` evaluates to `3`, not `3.5`. Getting a real fractional result requires at least one operand to already be a floating-point type, often via an explicit cast: `(double) 7 / 2` evaluates to `3.5` because the cast promotes `7` to a `double` *before* the division happens, so the division itself becomes floating-point division.

Relational operators (`== != < > <= >=`) produce a `boolean`, and logical operators (`&& || !`) combine booleans -- with `&&` and `||` specifically being **short-circuiting**: in `a && b`, if `a` is `false`, `b` is never even evaluated, because the overall result is already determined to be `false`. This isn't just an optimization detail -- it's a common, deliberate safety pattern: `if (obj != null && obj.getValue() > 0)` relies on short-circuiting to guarantee `obj.getValue()` is never called when `obj` is `null`, avoiding a `NullPointerException`. Writing `&` or `|` instead (the non-short-circuiting bitwise/logical operators) would evaluate both sides unconditionally and defeat that safety entirely. Compound assignment (`+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`) and increment/decrement (`++`, `--`) are shorthand you'll use constantly -- `count += 1;` and `count++;` both increment `count` by one, though they differ subtly when used as sub-expressions inside larger statements, which is worth being deliberate about rather than clever with.

sections.heading: == on Primitives vs Reference Types, and the String Trap
sections.body:
The `==` operator's behavior depends entirely on whether it's comparing primitives or references, and conflating the two is one of the most common bugs for people newer to Java. On primitives, `==` compares the actual values: `5 == 5` is `true` because both sides hold the identical numeric value. On reference types, `==` compares whether both operands point to the **exact same object in memory** -- not whether the two objects happen to contain equal content. Two separately-created objects with identical data are not `==` to each other; for content comparison, you need the `.equals()` method instead (covered properly once we reach classes and objects).

`String` makes this especially confusing at first because of a quirk called the **string literal pool**: string literals written directly in code (`"hello"`) are interned and reused, so two variables holding the same literal text often *do* end up pointing at the same pooled object, making `==` appear to 'work' by accident:

```java
String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
String c = new String("hello");

System.out.println(a == b);        // true  -- both point at the same pooled literal
System.out.println(a == c);        // false -- new String(...) forces a distinct heap object
System.out.println(a.equals(c));   // true  -- same characters, which is what usually matters
```

The safe habit to build now, before this becomes a live bug in real code, is: use `==` for primitives and for genuinely checking 'is this the same object,' and use `.equals()` whenever what you actually care about is 'do these hold the same content.'

examples.title: Primitives Are Copied, Arrays (and Objects) Are Aliased
examples.explanation: `int b = a;` copies the actual value 5 into b's own separate storage slot; from that point on, a and b are two completely independent int variables, so reassigning b never touches a. `int[] arr2 = arr1;` looks structurally identical, but arr1 is a reference variable, so this line copies the reference (the address) -- not the array's contents. arr1 and arr2 now both point at the one and only array object that exists; mutating an element through arr2 is visible through arr1 too, because there is genuinely only one array here, just two names for it. This is exactly the distinction that makes 'primitive vs reference' the most important type distinction in Java to internalize early.

examples.title: == vs .equals(): The String Literal Pool Trap
examples.explanation: a and b are both string literals with identical text, and Java's compiler and runtime intern string literals into a shared pool, so a and b actually end up referring to the exact same String object -- which is why a == b happens to be true here. c, however, is created with new String("hello"), which explicitly forces the creation of a brand-new object on the heap, deliberately bypassing the pool -- so even though c holds the same characters as a, it is a genuinely different object, and a == c correctly reports false. a.equals(c) is true because .equals() on String is specifically implemented to compare character content rather than object identity. The lesson is not 'avoid new String()' (which is rarely written in real code anyway) -- it's that == on any reference type, String included, is answering 'is this literally the same object', which is very often not the question you actually meant to ask.

examples.title: Integer Division, Casting, and the Remainder Operator
examples.explanation: total / count divides two int values, and Java's rule for integer division is to truncate toward zero rather than round -- 7 / 2 is mathematically 3.5, but the int result simply discards the fractional part, giving 3. Casting matters for exactly when it's applied: (double) total / count casts total to a double first, which means the division operator now sees a double and an int, promotes the int to a double too, and performs genuine floating-point division, yielding 3.5. Writing (double) (total / count) instead would cast the already-truncated result of 3 to 3.0 -- a completely different, and wrong, outcome, which is a common careless mistake. total % count gives the remainder of the integer division (7 = 3*2 + 1), which is often exactly what you want for tasks like checking evenness (n % 2 == 0) or wrapping an index around a fixed range.

misconceptions.description: == always checks whether two things are 'equal' in the everyday, content-based sense, the same way .equals() does.
misconceptions.clarification: == behaves completely differently depending on what it's comparing. On primitive types, there's no meaningful distinction between 'same value' and 'same object' -- a primitive variable just holds a value directly, so == comparing values is the only sensible behavior, and it works exactly as expected. On reference types, though, == compares object identity: whether both sides point at the exact same object in memory, not whether the objects hold equivalent content. Two separately-constructed objects holding identical data -- two separate Point objects both representing (3, 4), for instance -- are not == to each other. Content comparison for reference types is the job of .equals() (once a class defines it meaningfully), not ==.

misconceptions.description: Since Java requires you to write explicit types, using var in var x = 5; makes Java behave like a dynamically-typed language for that particular variable, letting it hold different types later.
misconceptions.clarification: var is purely a compile-time convenience that lets the compiler infer a variable's type from its initializer, so you don't have to write it out yourself -- it does not change how strictly that type is enforced afterward. Once var x = 5; runs, x's type is permanently int, decided once at compile time, exactly as if you had written int x = 5; by hand. Trying to later write x = "hello"; is still a compile-time type error, just like it would be for an explicitly-typed int. var changes what you type, not what Java's type system actually does.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and why?
hints: balances and backup are both arrays -- a reference type. What does assigning one array variable to another actually copy: the data, or the reference?
firstBalance and firstBalanceCopy are both plain int variables -- a primitive type. What does assignment copy in that case?
Track which of the two assignments (backup[1] = 999 vs firstBalanceCopy = -1) can possibly affect a variable other than the one directly on the left-hand side.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 999, then 100. balances and backup are the same underlying array (reference copy), so mutating it through backup is visible through balances too. firstBalance and firstBalanceCopy are independent int copies, so reassigning firstBalanceCopy has no effect on firstBalance.
exercises.solutionExplanation: int[] backup = balances; copies the array reference, not the array's contents -- balances and backup are two names for the one array object that exists. backup[1] = 999; mutates that single shared array, so reading balances[1] afterward correctly reflects the change: 999. Separately, int firstBalanceCopy = firstBalance; copies the primitive int value 100 into a brand-new, independent storage slot -- firstBalance and firstBalanceCopy have no ongoing connection after that assignment. Reassigning firstBalanceCopy to -1 only affects that one variable; firstBalance still holds its original value, 100, completely unaffected.

exercises.prompt: This method is supposed to check whether a user-entered command equals "quit", but it sometimes reports false even when the text is clearly "quit". Find and fix the bug.
hints: normalized is a String -- a reference type. What does == actually compare for reference types: content, or object identity?
"quit" as written here is a string literal, pulled from the interned literal pool. Is normalized guaranteed to be that exact same pooled object?
There's a method on String specifically designed to compare character content rather than object identity -- which one, and how should this return statement use it?
exercises.solutionExplanation: normalized == "quit" compares object identity, not text content -- and normalized is built via new String(...), which explicitly creates a brand-new heap object rather than reusing anything from the string literal pool. Even when normalized's characters are exactly "quit", it is never the same object as the literal "quit" used on the right-hand side, so == is false essentially every time, regardless of the actual text. The fix, normalized.equals("quit"), compares character content instead of object identity, which is what 'does this string say quit' actually means. This bug is a direct, practical instance of the == vs .equals() trap: it happens to look like it might work in quick testing (if you'd used a literal instead of new String(...), the literal pool could accidentally make == appear to succeed), which is exactly what makes it dangerous in real code.

assessments.prompt: int[] a = {1, 2, 3}; int[] b = a; b[0] = 100; What is a[0] after this runs, and why?
options: 1, because assigning b = a copies the array's contents into a brand-new, separate array for b.
100, because b = a copies the reference, so a and b refer to the exact same array object, and mutating it through either name is visible through the other.
0, because arrays are reset to their default values whenever a second reference is created.
This code fails to compile, because two array variables cannot refer to the same array.
assessments.explanation: Arrays are reference types, so int[] b = a; copies the reference (effectively, the address) stored in a into b -- it does not allocate a new array or copy any elements. a and b end up being two different variable names pointing at the one and only array object that was ever created. Mutating an element through b (b[0] = 100) mutates that shared object, so reading a[0] afterward correctly shows 100. Option A describes value-copy semantics, which apply to primitives, not arrays. Option C describes behavior that simply doesn't happen in Java. Option D is wrong because having multiple reference variables point at the same object is not just legal, it's one of the most fundamental and common things you do in Java.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to someone who has only used a dynamically-typed language before, the difference between a primitive variable and a reference variable in Java, and why that difference matters in practice (not just in theory).
assessments.modelAnswer: In Java, every variable is one of two kinds, and the difference is about what the variable's own storage location actually contains. A primitive variable -- int, double, boolean, char, and a few others -- holds its value directly: the bits representing that number or boolean are sitting right there in the variable's slot, with nothing indirect about it. A reference variable -- anything that's a class type, an array, or String -- does not hold the object itself; it holds a reference, essentially an address, pointing to where the real object actually lives, separately, typically on the heap. This stops being an abstract distinction the moment you assign one variable to another or pass one into a method. Assigning one primitive variable to another copies the value itself, producing two fully independent variables from then on -- changing one can never affect the other. Assigning one reference variable to another copies the reference, not the object, so both variables end up pointing at the identical object; mutating that object's state through either name is visible through the other name too, because there is really only one object involved, just two labels for it. This is exactly why an array passed into a method can have its elements changed by that method in a way the caller sees afterward, while an int passed into a method can never have its value changed from the caller's perspective -- the method only ever receives a copy of the int's value, with no ongoing connection back to the caller's variable. Coming from a language where 'variable' doesn't usually force you to think about this distinction so explicitly, the practical payoff is being able to correctly predict, just by knowing whether a type is primitive or a reference, whether a change made in one place in your code is going to be visible somewhere else.

assessments.prompt: Given String name = null; if (name != null && name.length() > 3) { System.out.println("long name"); }, why does this never throw a NullPointerException, even though name is null?
options: && and & behave identically in Java, so it wouldn't matter which one was used here.
&& short-circuits: because name != null evaluates to false, Java never evaluates the right-hand side name.length() > 3 at all, so the call that would otherwise throw is simply never made.
Java automatically inserts a null check before every method call, regardless of which logical operator is used in the surrounding expression.
name.length() quietly returns 0 instead of throwing whenever name is null, so the comparison is always false but never crashes.
assessments.explanation: && and || are short-circuiting: once the left operand of && is false, the overall result is already determined, so Java never bothers evaluating the right operand at all. That's precisely why name != null && name.length() > 3 is a safe, common idiom -- name.length() is only reached on the path where name is already known to be non-null. Option A is wrong and is the exact misconception this idiom guards against: & evaluates both sides unconditionally, so name != null & name.length() > 3 would call length() on a null reference and throw. Option C is wrong because Java has no such automatic null-checking mechanism. Option D is wrong because calling a method on a null reference throws NullPointerException; it does not return a default value.

assessments.prompt: What do (double) (9 / 2) and (double) 9 / 2 each evaluate to?
options: Both evaluate to 4.5, since casting to double anywhere in the expression forces the entire calculation to use floating-point division.

(double) (9 / 2) evaluates to 4.0, because the parenthesized integer division 9 / 2 truncates to 4 first, and only that already-truncated result gets cast to double; (double) 9 / 2 casts 9 to 9.0 before dividing, so the division itself is floating-point division, giving 4.5.
(double) (9 / 2) evaluates to 4.5 and (double) 9 / 2 evaluates to 4.0 -- the parentheses matter, but in the opposite direction from the previous option.
Both evaluate to 4, since casting an already-computed int result to double has no effect on its value.
assessments.explanation: Where the cast is placed changes when it takes effect. In (double) (9 / 2), the parentheses force 9 / 2 to be evaluated first as integer division, truncating toward zero to 4, and only that final int value gets cast to 4.0 -- the cast arrives too late to change how the division itself was performed. In (double) 9 / 2, the cast applies to 9 alone, promoting it to 9.0 before the division operator ever runs, which means the division sees a double and an int and performs genuine floating-point division, yielding 4.5. Option A is wrong because a cast only affects the operand it's directly attached to, not the whole expression. Option C reverses the correct pairing. Option D is wrong because 4.0 and 4 are numerically equal but the cast still changes the value's type and, in the other expression, its actual magnitude.

assessments.prompt: What happens when this method is compiled? public static void main(String[] args) { int total; System.out.println(total); }
options: It compiles fine and prints 0, since Java initializes every int variable to 0 by default.

It fails to compile with a "variable might not have been initialized" error, because local variables declared inside a method are never given an automatic default value -- unlike instance and static fields, which do get one.
It fails to compile because Java forbids declaring a variable and using it on separate statements.
It compiles fine but throws a NullPointerException the moment total is printed, since it has no value yet.
assessments.explanation: Local variables -- those declared inside a method -- are a deliberate exception to Java's default-value rules: they get no automatic initialization at all, and the compiler forces you to assign a value before the first read by rejecting the program outright if you don't. This is different from instance and static fields, which do receive automatic defaults (0 for numeric types, false for boolean, and so on) if left unassigned. Option A describes field defaults, not local variable behavior. Option C is wrong because declaring and later assigning a local variable across separate statements is completely normal; the issue here is reading before any assignment at all. Option D is wrong because this code never reaches run time in the first place -- javac rejects it before producing a .class file, so no exception is ever thrown.

concepts.title: The main Method: How a Java Program Starts and Runs
concepts.description: Every Java program needs exactly one method with the precise signature `public static void main(String[] args)` for the JVM to call as its entry point -- and each keyword in that signature is load-bearing, not boilerplate, for reasons rooted in how the JVM actually starts a program with no object yet in existence.
learningObjectives: State the exact required signature of the main method and explain why each modifier (public, static, void) and the String[] args parameter is necessary.
Explain how command-line arguments become the String[] args array, and what args looks like when no arguments are passed.
Explain what happens, and when, if a class has no valid main method, or if a program has several classes that each define one.
Predict program termination behavior for a normal return, an explicit System.exit call, and an uncaught exception.
Trace, at a beginner level, what it means for main to call other methods and for control to return back to main afterward.

sections.heading: The Exact Signature, and Why Every Word in It Is Necessary
Command-Line Arguments: From the Terminal to String[]
Finding the Entry Point: One JVM Invocation, One Chosen main
sections.body:
Nothing stops multiple classes in the same project from each defining their own `public static void main(String[] args)` -- there's no ambiguity at the language level, because you explicitly tell the JVM which class to start from when you invoke it: `java Greet` runs `Greet`'s main; `java Calculator` runs `Calculator`'s main, if it has one. Having several 'entry points' available in one codebase (common in small utility projects, or during learning, where each exercise might live in its own class with its own main) is completely normal.

What's worth understanding precisely is what happens when the class you name has *no* valid main -- because the signature is missing entirely, or subtly wrong (missing `static`, wrong parameter type, wrong capitalization). This is not a compile-time failure: `javac` doesn't require any class to have a main method at all, since not every class is meant to be a program's starting point (most classes in a real Java codebase never have one). The failure shows up only when you actually try to run that specific class with `java ClassName`, and the JVM's launcher looks for the exact signature and doesn't find it: `Error: Main method not found in class ClassName, please define the main method as: public static void main(String[] args)`. The code compiled just fine; it simply isn't runnable *as an entry point* the way you tried to run it.

sections.heading: Program Termination: Falling Off the End, System.exit, and Uncaught Exceptions

examples.title: Reading Command-Line Arguments Safely
examples.explanation: The args.length check comes first specifically to avoid indexing into an array that might be empty -- args[0] is only ever reached on a path where length is already known to be at least 1. Skipping that check and writing args[0] unconditionally would work fine when arguments happen to be supplied, and then throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException the moment someone runs the program with no arguments at all -- a bug that's easy to miss in casual testing (where you might always remember to pass an argument) and easy to hit in real usage (where users won't). Note also that args[0] here is treated purely as text; if this program needed Alice's age as a number instead of a name, it would need an explicit parse step, because every element of args is a String no matter what it looks like.

examples.title: A Wrong Signature Compiles Fine, But the JVM Can't Find It
examples.explanation: Broken.java compiles without any complaint, because public void main(String[] args) is a perfectly ordinary, syntactically valid instance method -- there's nothing illegal about defining it, and javac has no requirement that any particular class contain a runnable entry point. The failure only appears when java Broken is actually run: the launcher specifically looks for a static method matching the exact required signature, and this one isn't static, so it doesn't count as an entry point no matter how closely it otherwise resembles one. The underlying reason static is mandatory is concrete, not arbitrary: at the moment the JVM wants to call main, no instance of Broken has been created yet, and an instance method fundamentally cannot be called without an instance to call it on.

examples.title: Exit Codes: Normal Completion vs System.exit vs an Uncaught Exception
examples.explanation: Running this with no arguments prints the first two lines and then calls System.exit(1), which halts the JVM immediately at that exact point -- the third println and everything after it never execute, and the process reports exit code 1 to whatever launched it (a shell script checking $? or %ERRORLEVEL% would see that 1 and could branch on it). Running it with an argument of "0" gets past the exit check, reaches the division, and throws an uncaught ArithmeticException, which is a third, different way for the program to end: the JVM prints a stack trace to standard error and exits with a nonzero status, without ever reaching the final println. Running it with a genuine nonzero numeric argument like "5" runs every line to completion and exits normally with the implicit status 0. Three different endings for the same program, driven entirely by what's passed in and what happens along the way.

misconceptions.description: main is declared void just as a lazy default; it really ought to return something meaningful, the way a typical method does.
misconceptions.clarification: main genuinely has nothing meaningful to return a value to, in the way a normal method call does -- its caller is the JVM's own launcher, not other Java code sitting around ready to receive and use a return value. The way a Java program communicates a status back out to the operating system or a calling shell script is through a process exit code, produced either implicitly (0, on normal completion) or explicitly via System.exit(code) -- not through main's return type. Declaring main to return anything other than void would not compile at all; void isn't a placeholder for 'we haven't decided what to return yet,' it's the correct, permanent signature.

misconceptions.description: If a class has no main method, or has main with the wrong signature, javac will refuse to compile it.
misconceptions.clarification: This is a run-time failure, not a compile-time one. javac has no requirement that any class define a main method at all -- most classes in any real Java program never do, since most classes aren't meant to be a program's starting point. A class with no main, or with a subtly wrong signature (missing static, wrong capitalization, wrong parameter type), compiles completely successfully with javac. The failure only appears if and when you try to run that specific class as a program with java ClassName, and the JVM's launcher looks for the exact required signature and doesn't find it -- producing a runtime launch error, not anything javac ever objected to.

exercises.prompt: This program is meant to print a personalized greeting using the first command-line argument, but it crashes with ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException whenever it's run with no arguments. Find and fix the bug.
hints: What does args look like when the program is run with zero command-line arguments -- is it null, or something else?
Indexing args[0] assumes there's at least one element present. Is there anything in this code that actually guarantees that before the indexing happens?
Add a check on args.length before trying to read args[0], and decide what the program should print instead when there are no arguments at all.
exercises.solutionExplanation: When java Greet is run with no arguments, args is a real array with length 0 -- not null -- so args[0] is an attempt to read an element that simply doesn't exist, which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at run time (the compiler cannot know ahead of time how many arguments a user will actually supply, so it can't catch this). The fix checks args.length before indexing, falling back to a default name ("stranger") when no argument was provided, and only reading args[0] on the path where it's already known to be safe. This is the standard defensive pattern any time you read from args -- always guard the index with a length check rather than assuming a particular number of arguments will be present.

exercises.prompt: This program is run from the terminal as: java ReportTool alpha beta gamma. What does it print?
hints: Everything typed after the class name on the command line, separated by whitespace, becomes one element of args each -- how many words come after ReportTool here?
args[0] is the FIRST argument after the class name, not the class name itself -- the class name is never part of args.
Trace the loop for i = 0, 1, 2 exactly as written, printing the index and the corresponding args element each time.
exercises.solutionExplanation: java ReportTool alpha beta gamma passes exactly three command-line arguments -- alpha, beta, and gamma -- into args; the class name ReportTool itself is never included in args, it's just how the JVM knows which class's main to run. So args.length is 3, and the loop runs for i = 0, 1, 2, printing each index alongside the corresponding element: '0: alpha', '1: beta', '2: gamma', in that order, matching the order the arguments were typed on the command line.

assessments.prompt: Why must the main method be declared static?
options: static is required so that main can be called from other classes in the same package.
static means main belongs to the class itself rather than to any particular instance, which is essential because the JVM has to call main before any object of that class has ever been created.
static is only a performance optimization that makes main run slightly faster.
static is required by convention only; java ClassName would work identically without it.
assessments.explanation: Option B identifies the real, structural reason: at program start-up, the JVM needs to invoke main with no object of the class in existence yet, and only a static method can be called without an instance to call it on. Option A is wrong -- accessibility across packages is what public is for, not static, and static doesn't grant any package-related access on its own. Option C is wrong -- static has nothing to do with execution speed. Option D is wrong and worth flagging directly, since it's a tempting guess: omitting static causes java ClassName to fail at launch with 'Main method not found', because the launcher specifically requires a static method matching the exact signature -- it is not merely a style convention.

assessments.prompt: Explain the full contract the JVM expects from a program's entry point: the exact required signature, why each part of that signature is necessary, and the three ways a Java program can terminate.
assessments.modelAnswer: The JVM requires a method with the exact signature public static void main(String[] args) inside whichever class you name when you run java ClassName, and every part of that signature exists for a specific, concrete reason rather than as boilerplate. public is required because the JVM is calling this method from outside the class entirely, so the method has to be visible to an external caller. static is required because, at the moment the program starts, no instance of the class has been created yet -- there is no object for an instance method to be called on, and static methods are exactly the ones that can be invoked without one. void reflects that main doesn't hand a return value back to code that would consume it the way a normal method call does; its caller is the JVM's launcher, and a program instead communicates a completion status to the operating system through a process exit code. String[] args is always present as a parameter, holding whatever command-line arguments were supplied as an array of strings -- an empty array, not null, if none were given, and always strings even if the text looks numeric, requiring explicit parsing to use as a number. As for termination: a program can end by simply running to completion (falling off the end of main, or hitting a bare return), which exits with an implicit status of 0, meaning success by convention; it can end by explicitly calling System.exit(code), which halts execution immediately at that point, skipping everything after it, and reports whatever status code was passed; or it can end because an exception was thrown somewhere and never caught anywhere along the call chain back up to main, in which case the JVM prints a stack trace to standard error and exits with a nonzero status, signaling failure. All three are really the same underlying mechanism -- the JVM stops running the program and reports a status code -- triggered by three different circumstances.

assessments.prompt: A program is run as java Calc 5 10, where Calc's main contains: int result = args[0] + args[1]; System.out.println(result); What happens?
options: It compiles fine and prints 15, since args elements are automatically parsed to int whenever they're used in an arithmetic expression.

It fails to compile, because args[0] and args[1] are always String regardless of what the text looks like, so + performs string concatenation, producing a String value that cannot be assigned to an int variable.
It compiles fine and prints the text "510", because int is able to hold digit sequences produced by concatenation.
It compiles fine but throws NumberFormatException at run time, because "5" and "10" aren't recognized as valid int literals.
assessments.explanation: Every element of args is a String no matter what the command-line text looks like -- there is no automatic parsing to a numeric type. Applied to two String operands, + performs string concatenation, not addition, producing the String "510"; attempting to assign that String to a variable declared int is a compile-time type mismatch, so this program never produces a .class file at all. Option A is wrong because there is no implicit String-to-int conversion in Java. Option C is wrong because int cannot hold a String value regardless of what that string looks like -- this is exactly the error the compiler reports. Option D is wrong because the program never reaches run time in the first place; the failure is caught by javac before execution could ever begin.

assessments.prompt: Given this main method: public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("A"); if (args.length == 0) { System.exit(2); } System.out.println("B"); } -- run with zero command-line arguments, what prints and what exit status does the process report?
options: Prints A and B, then exits with status 0, because System.exit(2) only takes effect if no output has already been produced.
Prints only A -- the JVM halts immediately at the point System.exit(2) is called, skipping the second println entirely -- and the process reports exit status 2.
Prints A, then throws an uncaught exception, because System.exit requires args to be non-empty.
Fails to compile, because System.exit may only be called with the values 0 or 1.
assessments.explanation: With zero arguments, args.length == 0 is true, so System.exit(2) executes right after "A" is printed. System.exit terminates the JVM immediately at the exact point it's called, skipping every remaining statement -- including the second println -- and reports whatever integer was passed, 2, as the process's exit status. Option A is wrong because System.exit takes effect the instant it's called, regardless of prior output. Option C is wrong because System.exit takes an int status code as its parameter, and calling it has nothing to do with args being empty or not -- it runs unconditionally once reached. Option D is wrong because System.exit accepts any int value as a status code, not just 0 or 1; those are only conventional meanings, not enforced restrictions.
